transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?
I’m constantly worrying about everything—my kids, my job, money—and it feels like it never lets up. It’s just reached a point where I feel completely overwhelmed and don't know how to turn it off.

Did these worries start after a specific stressful life event or major change, or have they been going on across many areas of life even without one clear trigger? About how long has this been happening?

It started a little over a year ago when I was going through a difficult divorce and simultaneously took on a high-pressure digital transformation project at work. While those were the triggers, the anxiety has since spread to almost every area of my life, like my finances and parenting, and it hasn't let up since.

Now that the divorce and work crisis have changed or passed, do you still feel this excessive worry most days, even when there isn’t a specific stressor going on? Or does the anxiety mainly flare up only in response to those ongoing life stresses?

Yes, I feel it pretty much every day, even when there isn't an active crisis going on. Even during relaxing times, like when I'm out for a hike or hanging out with friends, my mind still cycles through endless "what-if" scenarios. It just feels completely impossible to turn off, no matter what I'm doing.

Along with the constant worry, have you also been having physical or mental symptoms like feeling restless or on edge, getting tired easily, trouble concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, or problems sleeping? If so, which ones have been happening most days?

I definitely feel restless and physically tense, almost like I have a motor running inside me, and I'm constantly pacing or clenching my jaw. I've also been really irritable, snapping at my son and coworkers over minor things, and my sleep is awful because I lie awake for hours replaying worries and wake up completely exhausted.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports excessive, difficult-to-control worry occurring most days for over a year across multiple life domains, persisting even without an active stressor, along with associated restlessness, muscle tension, irritability, and sleep disturbance. This pattern is most consistent with generalized anxiety disorder rather than a time-limited adjustment reaction.
